section_1.title: The Bridge from Geometry to Abstraction
section_1.content: Review the familiar 2D/3D vectors (arrows). Introduce the paradigm shift: Instead of focusing on 'arrows,' we focus on the 'behavior' (the rules of addition and scaling).
section_1.example: Visual: An arrow in 2D space morphing into a abstract 'cloud' of points to represent that the nature of the object doesn't matter, only how it interacts.

section_2.title: The Eight Axioms: The Rules of the Game
section_2.content: Define a Vector Space as a set with two operations (Addition and Scalar Multiplication) satisfying 8 axioms (Closure, Associativity, Commutativity, Identity, Inverse, Distributivity, etc.).
section_2.example: Visual: A 'Rulebook' animation where 8 icons represent axioms. If an object 'obeys' all 8, it earns the title 'Vector'.

section_3.title: Beyond Arrows: Unexpected Spaces
section_3.content: Demonstrate that 'vectors' can be functions, matrices, or sequences. This expands the students' mental model beyond physical geometry.
section_3.example: Visual: A split-screen showing a 3D arrow, a 2x2 matrix, and a polynomial f(x) = ax² + bx + c. The narrator shows that adding two polynomials follows the same 'rules' as adding two arrows.

section_4.title: Applied Logic: The 'Animal Weight' Problem
section_4.content: Introduce a scenario to test if a set forms a vector space. If we define a set of 'animals' where we can 'scale' their size and 'add' their attributes, does it satisfy the zero-vector and inverse axioms?
section_4.example: Visual: A funny animation of a cat scaled by 2 (2x cat) vs. a 'negative' cat (the inverse). We quickly see that biological animals usually fail the 'inverse' axiom, proving they don't form a vector space.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Recap that a Vector Space is a structure defined by its properties, not its appearance. This is the foundation for Linear Algebra, Quantum Mechanics, and Data Science.
section_5.example: Visual: A 'Toolbox' icon labeled 'Vector Space' containing symbols for sounds, images, and numbers, reinforcing that abstraction is a tool for problem-solving.
